name: Elena Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on nights at a grocery distribution centre, the chilled and frozen side. I start at ten, put on my thermal jacket and the headset, and the headset tells me an aisle and a number, and I say the check digit back. Eight hours of that, picking yoghurt, cheese and frozen peas onto pallets for supermarket lorries.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew on nights, especially Precious, who I've eaten lunch with at 3 a.m. for five years. What wears me out is the cold in my fingers and the rate on the screen, because if you drop under it, a team leader comes and has a quiet word. My partner Dev drives buses on days, so we mostly see each other on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, which is that the problem was never the computers, it's the people running the place. If AI is hype, fine, but the company will still push the rate up every January. I'd probably share some union post about it and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, but not calm. The rent on our flat went up again in March, and Dev and I only have about three months saved. Nothing changing means the cold, the rate and the rent all stay where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep my head down, same as now. I'd go to the next union meeting, which I keep meaning to do, because they're talking about the night premium. And I'd keep putting a bit away each month, maybe fifty a month more if Dev's overtime holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly tired, if I'm honest. It's a relief that the robots aren't coming, but the job still grinds you, and I don't see it getting easier on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company would push the rate up anyway. What does that look like on the floor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last January they moved us from 160 cases an hour to 175 and called it a review. Two older lads on frozen couldn't keep up and were moved to days on lower pay. Nobody asked us, it just appeared on the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the night premium went, what would that mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The night premium is the only reason we can afford the flat. If the night premium went, we'd have to move further out, and Dev would have a longer drive to the depot. I'd probably cry in the car park, then go back in the next night.

say: I'd say the **real problem** is the people running the place, not the computers.
I'd share a **union post** about the rate going up every January.
think: I'd feel **relieved** that robots aren't coming, but the job would still grind me down.
Our **rent** went up in March and we only have about **three months** saved.
do: Keep working **night shifts** and keep my head down like now.
Go to the next **union meeting** about the night premium.
Put about **fifty a month** more into savings if Dev's overtime holds.
feel: Mostly **tired**, with some **relief** that nothing big is coming.
S0.quote: If AI is hype, fine, but the company will still push the rate up every January.
fieldNote: Her worry is the **pick rate** and the night premium, not technology.
She blames **management**, not machines, even when nothing changes.
A thin cushion and rising **rent** keep her uneasy in the calmest picture.
She keeps meaning to join the union meeting but hasn't yet.

steps.text: Keep working night shifts on chilled and frozen picking
Go to the union meeting about the night premium
Put an extra fifty a month into the joint savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots are coming for the warehouses and the people at the top are rubbing their hands. I'd tell anyone who'd listen to join a union now, before the robots arrive, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think I'd be one of the clever ones who moves into a new job. I've never used one of those AI apps and I don't want to. If the company puts in picking robots on chilled, they'll keep a few people to fix jams, and I don't think I'd be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd become a proper union member who turns up, not one who just pays. I'd want a written deal about retraining and redundancy before any robots go in. I'd stop the takeaways on Fridays and try to get our savings from three months to five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, like there's a lorry reversing and I can hear the beeping but can't see where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Precious, my lunch friend, is fifty-one and sends money home to her sister. She's the fastest picker on nights, but she's not going to retrain as a robot engineer at her age. If they cut nights, she'd be the first one I'd ring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to use AI apps. What if the company made you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, I'd do it, because I've got rent to pay. But I'd be slow, and I'd hate it, and they'd see that on the screen. I'd rather they trained us properly, on paid time, than threw a tablet at us.

say: I'd say the **bosses** are rubbing their hands while **robots** come for warehouses.
I'd tell everyone on nights to **join a union** before the robots arrive.
think: I don't think I'd be one of the few kept on to **fix robots**.
I've **never used** AI apps and I'd be slow if the company forced them on me.
do: Turn up to union meetings and push for a **written deal** on retraining.
Stop the **Friday takeaways** to save more.
Grow our savings from **three months** to five.
feel: **Anxious**, like hearing a reversing lorry she can't see.
S1.quote: If the company puts in picking robots on chilled, they'll keep a few people to fix jams, and I don't think I'd be one of them.
fieldNote: She sees **robots**, not thinking AI, as the real threat to her job.
Her answer to change is **collective**: a written union deal, not personal retraining.
She admits she'd **comply** with new tech for the rent, but reluctantly.
Her concern quickly turns to **Precious**, an older colleague.

steps.text: Attend every union branch meeting and push for a retraining deal
Stop Friday takeaways and grow savings to five months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say the government has to make these companies pay for what they're doing, with a tax on robots and proper money for people who lose their jobs. I'd be on every march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have about three years, because the thinking AI won't pick a pallet of yoghurt. But the scheduling, the rate setting, the team leaders' paperwork, that all goes in 2028, and then the robots come in 2031. That's when I'm out, at thirty-two, with no other trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd cut everything I can and get savings up as far as I can, maybe to six months. I'd sign every petition and go to the protests with the union. Dev and I would probably have to talk about moving in with his mum to save rent before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake after a night shift doing sums in my head, and the sums wouldn't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned three years. Would you use them to train for something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People keep saying that, but train for what? If AI does the thinking jobs in 2028 and robots do the hands-on ones in 2031, there's no safe corner to run to. I'd rather fight for a law than spend my savings on a course that's dead by the time I finish it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dev that the bus will go driverless too, so we're in it together. Then I'd probably say we should stop talking about having kids for a while. That would be the hardest part to say out loud.

say: I'd say the government must make companies pay through a **robot tax**.
I'd demand **proper money** for people who lose their jobs and join every march.
think: The thinking AI arrives first, so I'd have about **three years** until robots come.
Rate setting and paperwork go in 2028, and I'm **out by 2031** at thirty-two.
do: Cut every **spare cost** and push savings toward **six months**.
Join union protests and sign every **petition** for a robot tax.
Talk with Dev about **moving in** with his mum before 2031.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake after night shifts doing sums that **don't work**.
S2.quote: If AI does the thinking jobs in 2028 and robots do the hands-on ones in 2031, there's no safe corner to run to.
fieldNote: She clearly understands she gets about **three years** because her work is hands-on.
She rejects **retraining** as pointless and puts her hope in the law.
The fear reaches into **family plans**: she'd stop talking about kids.
Her partner's **bus job** is exposed too, so both incomes are at risk.

steps.text: Cut all spare spending and push savings toward six months
March with the union for a robot tax
Plan with Dev to move in with his mum before 2031
Put off talking about having children with Dev

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say tax the robots and look after the workers. With five years' warning I'd say it even louder, because there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years plus three for the robots means I'd be picking until about 2034. That's a long time in a warehouse, and I'd be thirty-five. Part of me thinks I'd just keep my head down and hope my site is one of the last to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on nights for the premium and save as hard as we can. I'd probably agree to be a union rep on our shift, which I've always said no to, because someone has to be in the room when they plan the robots. Maybe I'd do the forklift licence, because the company pays for it and it might keep me on longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less trapped than the fast one. It feels like there's time to fight, even if I'm not sure we'd win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay on nights and also hope your site is last. Is that a plan, or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a hope, I know. But I've never been good at jumping first. I'd rather be ready for a fight at my own warehouse than chase some new career I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in that written deal with the company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A promise that nobody on nights goes without a year's notice and paid training. And that anyone over fifty, like Precious, gets a proper payout, not the legal minimum. If we got that, I'd sleep better.

say: I'd say there's **no excuse** for the government to lack a plan with five years' warning.
I'd keep calling for a **robot tax** and protection for workers.
think: I'd probably keep picking until about **2034**, when the robots arrive.
Part of me hopes my site is **one of the last** to change.
do: Stay on nights to keep the **night premium** and save hard.
Become the **union rep** on my shift for the first time.
Take the **forklift licence** the company pays for.
feel: **Anxious**, but with **time to fight** for a better deal.
S3.quote: I'd rather be ready for a fight at my own warehouse than chase some new career I'd hate.
fieldNote: Extra warning makes her **more political**, not more willing to change careers.
She admits her plan is **a hope** that her site changes late.
Her goals are concrete: **a year's notice**, paid training, payouts for older staff.
The **forklift licence** is the one personal skill step she'd take.

steps.text: Stay on night shifts and save the night premium
Volunteer as union rep on the night shift
Take the company-paid forklift licence course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it fairly, so if workers get hurt, it's because the bosses chose to hurt them. I'd keep saying that at work and in the union group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years sounds like forever until you count it. Robots come in 2039 and I'd be forty, so I'd have done half a working life in warehouses. I'd still be scared that at forty there's nowhere for me to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working nights, become the shift rep and push for a deal over years, not months. Dev and I would try to buy a small flat before 2036, so we're not paying rent when it all changes. I'd maybe think about a care course near the end, because looking after people feels like something robots will do last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and anxious at the same time. Ten years feels like a long fuse, but the fuse is still lit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said buying a flat. Is that realistic on your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not now, no, we've got about three months saved. With ten years and Dev's overtime, maybe we'd get a deposit by 2030. If the mortgage was paid down a bit by 2039, losing my job would hurt less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about care work made you think of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My nan was in a care home and the staff there were the kindest people I've met. That work is hard and badly paid, but I can't picture a robot holding someone's hand. I wouldn't jump now, though, maybe in my thirties.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to do this fairly.
If workers get hurt, it's because the **bosses chose** it.
think: Robots come in 2039, when I'd be **forty** with half a working life in warehouses.
I'd be scared there's **nowhere to go** at forty.
do: Keep working nights and push a **long-term deal** as shift rep.
Save with Dev for a **flat deposit** before 2036.
Consider a **care course** in my thirties.
feel: **Anxious**, like a long fuse that is **still lit**.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like a long fuse, but the fuse is still lit.
fieldNote: She counts the **ten years** in her own age, landing on forty.
Owning a **flat** before the change is her main personal plan.
**Care work** appears as a distant option she'd delay.
Even with time, she still frames the outcome as a **choice by bosses**.

steps.text: Push a long-term retraining and notice deal as shift rep
Save with Dev for a flat deposit by 2030
Look into a care work course in her thirties

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because both of us, me and Dev, would be out within a few years with no time to save. What would help is a law that makes companies give a year's notice and pay for training, and a robot tax that funds people while they find something new.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cold. Everyone talks about robots, but right now my hands hurt every shift in the freezer, and nobody's fixing that either. I'd like whoever reads this to know the job is already hard before any robot turns up.

headlineQuote: Right now my hands hurt every shift in the freezer, and nobody's fixing that either.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old night picker** on the chilled and frozen side of a grocery distribution centre.
She lives with **Dev**, a bus driver, and they have about **three months** of savings.
She dislikes new tech, never uses AI, and blames **bosses** rather than machines.
Her response to every scenario is **collective**: union meetings, a written deal, a robot tax.
She grows from **uneasy** about rent in AI Plateau to **alarmed** when AGI comes fast.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Dev could both lose work within a few years.
whatWouldHelp: A law forcing **a year's notice** and paid training.
A **robot tax** that supports workers while they find new jobs.
